lab_title: The Mars Loop: Understanding Apparent Retrograde Motion
top_level_objectives: Observe and describe the apparent retrograde motion of Mars against the background stars over a period of weeks
Explain why the geocentric model required epicycles to account for retrograde motion
Demonstrate how the heliocentric model naturally produces retrograde loops through the relative motion of Earth and Mars
Relate the apparent backward drift of an outer planet to the everyday experience of overtaking a slower-moving car
Compare the retrograde behavior of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and connect differences to orbital distance and relative speed

scenes.brief_purpose: Hook students with the historical mystery and establish what 'normal' planetary motion looks like before introducing the anomaly.
key_visuals: A night sky dome filled with recognizable zodiac constellations arching overhead
A bright reddish point of light labeled 'Mars' positioned against the stars
A subtle eastward-pointing arrow indicating Mars's usual slow drift
student_actions: Look around the immersive night sky and locate the labeled Mars
Read a short framing prompt asking them to predict how Mars will move over the coming weeks
Tap Mars to confirm its current position and begin the observation sequence

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students directly witness apparent retrograde motion by tracking Mars night after night from Earth's surface.
key_visuals: A time-lapse of the night sky advancing date-by-date with a visible calendar readout
A glowing trail left behind by Mars that bends into a westward loop and then resumes eastward
The fixed background constellations staying still as Mars traces its path
student_actions: Advance time using a slider to move the sky forward week by week
Mark on the trail where Mars appears to slow, stop, reverse, and resume
Record in a short prompt how many weeks the backward motion lasted

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how ancient astronomers explained the loop within an Earth-centered cosmos, highlighting the awkwardness of epicycles.
key_visuals: Earth at the center with Mars riding on a small circle (epicycle) attached to a larger circular path (deferent)
An animated tracing of the looping path the epicycle produces as seen from Earth
Labels identifying 'deferent' and 'epicycle'
student_actions: Watch the epicycle animation produce the same loop observed in the previous scene
Adjust the epicycle size and notice how it must be tuned to match the observation
Answer a reflection prompt on why this model felt complicated to its critics

scenes.brief_purpose: Reorient students to a heliocentric, bird's-eye view so they can see the true orbital motions of Earth and Mars.
key_visuals: The Sun at the center with Earth and Mars on their separate circular orbits
A clear difference in orbital radius and orbital speed between the faster inner Earth and slower outer Mars
A faint sightline drawn from Earth through Mars out to the background stars
student_actions: Rotate and zoom the orbital diagram to view it from above and from the side
Press play to watch both planets orbit at their real relative speeds
Identify which planet moves faster and note it in a prompt

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the outside view to the Earth view, revealing that the loop is an illusion created when Earth overtakes Mars.
key_visuals: The heliocentric orbits animating while the projected sightline sweeps across the background stars
A side-by-side mini-panel showing the resulting apparent path of Mars tracing the same loop
Highlighted moment where Earth passes Mars and the projected position appears to move backward
student_actions: Step through the overtaking moment frame by frame
Watch the sightline projection draw the retrograde loop in real time
Confirm that the heliocentric loop matches the loop they recorded from Earth

scenes.brief_purpose: Reinforce the relative-motion concept with an everyday experience to cement intuition.
key_visuals: A first-person view from inside a faster car passing a slower car on a highway
The slower car appearing to drift backward against distant scenery as it is overtaken
A linked overlay comparing the car scene to the Earth-overtaking-Mars scene
student_actions: Ride along as the faster car overtakes the slower one and observe the apparent backward drift
Toggle between the car analogy and the orbital animation to map the parallels
Answer a prompt explaining the analogy in their own words

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the principle by comparing Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, linking loop size to orbital distance and relative speed.
key_visuals: Three orbital diagrams or a single system showing Earth alongside Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
Apparent paths for each outer planet, with Mars looping dramatically and Saturn looping subtly
A small comparison chart of orbital distance versus retrograde loop size
student_actions: Select each planet to view and trace its retrograde loop
Rank the three planets by how dramatic their loops appear
Complete a concluding prompt explaining why more distant planets loop less
